summary: Presents a practical framework for measuring end-to-end TCP throughput in a managed IP network, aiming to give a better sign of what users experience. It specifies TCP and IP parameters to optimize throughput testing.

plainLanguage.summary: Measuring how fast a link is does not tell you how fast a user's data will actually arrive, because TCP has to ramp up and back off when packets are lost. This RFC sets out a way to measure the speed a user really gets, and what to report about it.

subtitle: A repeatable way to measure the speed a user actually gets on a managed network, and the three numbers to report.

tldr.problem: Service level agreements are written in terms of bandwidth, latency, loss and jitter, and measuring those does not tell you whether a user's data actually arrives quickly.
tldr.mechanism: The framework gives a three-step method: find the path MTU, measure the baseline round-trip time and bottleneck bandwidth, then run single and multiple connection throughput tests with the socket buffers sized to match.
tldr.outcome: It defines three metrics for the results, the transfer time ratio, the efficiency percentage and the buffer delay percentage, and a list of the host and network settings to check when the numbers are poor.

today: RFC 6349 is an Informational document published in August 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a testing methodology rather than a protocol: it says how to measure, what to report and what to check when the numbers are poor.

sections.title: Why Measure TCP Throughput at All
sections.content:
The service level agreements that network providers give business customers are usually written in terms of layer 2 and 3 criteria: bandwidth, latency, packet loss and jitter. Providers have come to realise that measuring those is not enough to be sure end users are satisfied, and this framework sets out a method for measuring TCP throughput as well, so that the results mean something about the user's experience. Business customers also want to run repeatable throughput tests between their own locations, and since they rely on the provider's network, a common method with agreed metrics serves both sides.

The focus is on managed business-class IP networks, such as Ethernet-terminated services covered by a service level agreement, where the expectation is that TCP throughput reaches the guaranteed bandwidth. Users on best-effort access could use the method, but the metrics only make sense in a predictable managed network, and no end-to-end performance can be guaranteed when only the access portion is provisioned to a particular bandwidth.

The quantity being measured is sustained TCP layer performance: the amount of data per unit of time that TCP transports when it is in the equilibrium state, meaning the steady state after the initial ramp-up, where the congestion window has settled. Throughout the document, maximum achievable throughput means the theoretical value when TCP is in that state.

Two window sizes decide how fast that can be. TCP is connection oriented, and the sending side uses a congestion window, while the receiving end uses a receive window to say how many bytes it can accept at a time. From the round-trip time and the bottleneck bandwidth of the path, the bandwidth-delay product gives the send and receive socket buffer sizes needed for maximum throughput. The congestion window is then worked out from the loss rate on the path using slow start and congestion avoidance. Whichever is smaller, the congestion window and the receive window advertised by the far end, decides how many bytes can actually be in flight at any moment. Both window sizes can vary during a session, but up to the bandwidth limit, larger windows give higher throughput because more data can be in flight at once.

Each end of a connection has default socket buffer sizes and kernel-enforced maximums, and some stacks use receive window auto-tuning. To get maximum throughput it is critical for the send and receive socket buffers to be large enough, and they should be at least the bandwidth-delay product. The method therefore concentrates on the bottleneck bandwidth, the round-trip time, the send and receive socket buffers, the minimum receive window, and the path MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring how fast a link is does not tell you how fast a user's data will actually arrive, because TCP has to ramp up and back off when packets are lost. This RFC sets out a way to measure the speed a user really gets.

sections.title: What the Method Does and Does Not Try to Do
sections.content:
Four things are ruled out. The method does not predict the throughput during the transient stages of a connection, such as the slow start phase. It does not definitively benchmark TCP implementations of one operating system against another, although some users may find qualitative experiments useful. It does not give a detailed diagnosis of problems inside the endpoints or inside the network, though interpreting each test step may point at likely issues. And it does not propose operating permanently with high measurement loads; performance and optimisation in an operational network may be captured and evaluated instead from the data in the TCP Extended Statistics MIB.

The primary goal is a practical end-to-end assessment of sustained TCP performance within a managed business-class IP network. The other key goal is a set of best practices that a person who is not a TCP expert should apply when validating that a managed network can carry end-user TCP applications.

The specific goals are a practical test approach that names the tunable parameters, such as the MTU and the socket buffer sizes, and shows how they affect TCP performance; specific test conditions, such as link speed, round-trip time, MTU and socket buffer sizes, with worked examples of the maximum achievable throughput; three basic metrics for comparing TCP performance under different network conditions; and a list of the areas in the end host or the network that should be looked at when the recommended procedure does not reach the maximum achievable throughput, without claiming to diagnose them properly.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is deliberately narrow. It measures the steady state, it does not compare operating systems, it does not diagnose faults, and it is not meant to run permanently on a live network.

sections.title: The Three Steps of a Test
sections.content:
Before measuring anything, the integrity of the network should be verified with layer 2 and 3 tests, and this is required, because a meaningful TCP measurement is impossible on a network that is not working: as a guideline, 5% packet loss or 150 ms of jitter is too high for an accurate measurement. Testing may need the cooperation of the customer and the provider, and on an MPLS network the test should be run on the customer equipment or the customer edge device rather than on the provider edge router.

There are three steps. First, identify the path MTU, running packetization layer path MTU discovery, so the test device can be configured to avoid fragmentation. Second, establish the baseline round-trip time and bottleneck bandwidth, which are used to estimate the receive window and send socket buffer sizes for the later steps. Third, run the TCP connection throughput tests, single and multiple, to baseline the network's performance.

The test device itself has requirements. It may be an ordinary computer or a dedicated instrument, but it must be able to act as both client and server, and it must be able to generate and receive stateful TCP traffic at the full bottleneck bandwidth of the network under test. Stateful means a full TCP/IP stack, which is a warning aimed at equipment that simply blasts packets with TCP headers; at the time of writing, testing above 100 Mbps may need high-performance server hardware or dedicated tools. Both send and receive socket buffer sizes must be adjustable and large enough to fill the bandwidth-delay product. Measuring round-trip time and retransmissions per connection will generally need dedicated hardware, or else packet captures analysed after the fact, or the TCP Extended Statistics MIB.

The path MTU. Path MTU discovery relies on ICMP messages to learn the path MTU: a device with the Don't Fragment bit set whose packet is too large for the next hop has the packet dropped and an ICMP message sent back carrying the next-hop MTU. Because many network managers disable ICMP entirely, this is not always reliable, so packetization layer path MTU discovery, which works with or without ICMP, must then be run to verify the path MTU, with the goal of avoiding fragmentation in all later tests.

The round-trip time. Round-trip time is the elapsed time between the clocking in of the first bit of a TCP segment sent and the receipt of the last bit of the matching acknowledgement. It should be baselined during off-peak hours, to get the inherent latency rather than delay caused by buffering, and when sampling over an interval the minimum measured value should be used. The document lists the ways to measure it in order of decreasing accuracy: test equipment at each end looping the far-end tester so a packet stream is measured back and forth; packet captures of TCP test sessions analysed for the round-trip time, though results based on the SYN to SYN-ACK at the start of a session should be avoided because firewalls slow down three-way handshakes; statistics from the MIBs in RFC 4898; and ICMP pings, which may need different packet sizes and are less reliable and less accurate than in-band measurements.

The bottleneck bandwidth. Before any TCP test, bandwidth measurement with stateless IP streams should be run to determine the bottleneck bandwidth of the network under test, in both directions, especially on asymmetrical access such as ADSL, and at various intervals through a business day or across a week. The tests should produce logged outputs of the achieved bandwidths across the whole test duration.

The window size. The minimum receive window is calculated from the bandwidth-delay product, which is the round-trip time in seconds multiplied by the bottleneck bandwidth in bits per second; dividing that by 8 gives the minimum receive window in bytes. For optimal results the send socket buffer must be adjusted to the same value at each end. As an example, on a T3 link with a 25 ms round-trip time the product is about 1,105,000 bits and the minimum receive window about 138 KB. Separate calculations are required on asymmetrical paths: a 90 ms ADSL line with 5 Mbps downstream and 640 Kbps upstream gives a downstream product of about 450,000 bits and an upstream one of only about 57,600 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The order matters. First find the largest packet that fits without being split, then measure how long a round trip takes and how fast the path really is, then run the transfer test with buffers sized for those numbers.

sections.title: The Three Metrics
sections.content:
Each direction of each test has to yield three numbers.

The TCP Transfer Time Ratio compares the actual transfer time with the ideal one. The ideal transfer time for a given payload is the payload size in bits divided by the maximum achievable throughput, and the ratio is the actual time over the ideal time. The RFC's example moves 100 MB over five simultaneous connections where the Ethernet service provides a committed access rate of 500 Mbps: the ideal time would be about 8 seconds, the actual was 12, so the ratio is 1.5, meaning the transfer across all the connections took one and a half times as long as it should.

TCP Efficiency is the percentage of bytes that were not retransmitted: transmitted bytes minus retransmitted bytes, divided by transmitted bytes, times 100. Transmitted bytes means the total number of TCP bytes sent, including the original and the retransmitted ones. So if 100,000 bytes were sent and 2,000 had to be retransmitted, the efficiency is 98.03%. A byte that was retransmitted more than once counts again in both totals.

Buffer Delay Percentage is how much the round-trip time grew during the transfer compared with the baseline. The average round-trip time during the transfer is the total of all measured round-trip times divided by the transfer duration in seconds, and the percentage is the difference from the baseline divided by the baseline. With a baseline of 25 ms and an average of 32 ms during the transfer, the buffer delay is 28%.

All three have to be measured in each test. A poor transfer time ratio, meaning the actual time is longer than the ideal, can often be explained by correlating it with a poor efficiency percentage, which points at packet loss, or with a high buffer delay percentage, which points at congestion raising the round-trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: Three numbers come out of every test: how long the transfer took compared with the ideal, how much of the data had to be sent again, and how much the round-trip time grew. Together they say whether the network or the endpoints are at fault.

sections.title: Running the Tests and Reading the Results
sections.content:
The common tool is iperf, with a host at each end of the path, one acting as client and the other as server, and the send socket buffer and receive window sizes on both sides set by hand. For high bandwidth-delay product paths in lossy networks, such as long fat networks or satellite links, options such as selective acknowledgement should be part of the window size characterisation.

Host hardware performance has to be understood before the tests run, and a dedicated instrument will generally be required for gigabit and 10-gigabit line rates. The test should be coordinated with the provider if the expected throughput would exceed the customer's service level agreement, and it should run for long enough to exercise the network buffers properly, that is, for more than 30 seconds, and at different times of the day.

Whether to use one connection or several depends on the size of the bandwidth-delay product relative to the receive window configured in the end-user environment. If the product for a long fat network turns out to be 2 MB, it is more realistic to test that path with several connections. With typical host receive windows of 64 KB, 32 connections would emulate a small office. The RFC gives a table for a 500 Mbps network with a 5 ms round-trip time, where the product is 312.5 KB: 16 KB windows need 20 connections to fill the bandwidth, 32 KB need 10, 64 KB need 5, and 128 KB need 3.

At the end, the test device should produce a report with the calculated bandwidth-delay product and the window size experiments, giving achievable against actual throughput for each window size tested with no fragmentation, together with the three metrics. The point is to relate the metrics to user experience: the same transfer time ratio can be reached with a better efficiency at the cost of higher buffer delay.

Where the results fall short of the ideal, the RFC lists the likely causes: network congestion causing packet loss, which shows up as a poor efficiency percentage; network congestion causing an increase in round-trip time, which shows up in the buffer delay percentage; intermediate devices that regenerate the TCP connection and can alter the receive window or the MTU; rate limiting by policing rather than shaping; maximum TCP buffer space, since operating systems limit how much memory TCP may use and the limit may be far too small for a high-performance network; socket buffer sizes, which must be large enough to hold a full bandwidth-delay product plus overhead, and which TCP auto-tuning adjusts automatically; the TCP window scale option, which lets TCP support window sizes above 64 KB and can only be negotiated in the three-way handshake, so a client that wants to send at high rates may need to set a larger receive buffer before opening the connection; the TCP timestamps option, which improves round-trip time measurement and protects against late delivery; and selective acknowledgements, which let the receiver say exactly which segment is missing rather than making TCP guess, at the cost of the risk that a security appliance randomising TCP will break it. Both ends of a TCP connection must be properly tuned.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the test long enough to fill the buffers, at different times of day, and check both ends are tuned. The report should say how long the transfer took against the ideal, how much had to be resent, and how much the round-trip time grew.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Measuring TCP network performance raises security concerns, and the metrics produced within this framework may create them.

Denial of service. The metrics fill the network under test with a stateful connection, but since the test may use stateless IP streams as well, it might look to network operators like a denial-of-service attack. TCP throughput testing may therefore require cooperation between the customer and the provider.

User data confidentiality. The metrics generate packets from a sample rather than taking samples based on user data, so the framework does not threaten user data confidentiality.

Interference with metrics. The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks apply here as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A test that fills the link with traffic can look like an attack, so the provider should know it is happening. The measurements do not read anyone's data.

THE THREE STEPS OF THE METHODOLOGY

items.title: 1. Find the path MTU
items.text: Run packetization layer path MTU discovery so the test device can avoid fragmenting packets.

items.title: 2. Baseline RTT and bandwidth
items.text: Measure the round-trip time off peak and the bottleneck bandwidth in both directions.

items.title: 3. Run the throughput tests
items.text: Run single and multiple connection tests and record the three metrics in each direction.
